title: Amazon Filed for 10,000 H-1B Visas While Cutting 100,000 Tech Jobs. The Diaspora Is Caught in the Crossfire.
excerpt: A viral social-media firestorm exposes the brutal contradiction at the heart of America's skilled-immigration system — and Indian workers are bearing the brunt
body:
When investor James Fishback posted on X last week that Amazon had applied for 10,781 H-1B visas, the reaction was volcanic. "They don't want to hire you, your kids, or your grandkids," he wrote. "They want to hire cheap foreign laborers." The post, viewed more than 400,000 times, crystallised a contradiction that has been festering in Silicon Valley all year: America's biggest technology companies are simultaneously shedding tens of thousands of workers and filing for thousands of foreign-worker visas.

The numbers are stark. In the first five months of 2026, the technology sector has cut between 93,000 and 126,000 jobs globally, depending on the tracker. Meta slashed roughly 8,000 positions in April alone. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to seven per cent of its American workforce. Amazon has been trimming corporate roles in rolling waves. AI-driven efficiency — the very technology these companies are building — is the most commonly cited reason, accounting for more than a quarter of all announced cuts.

## The 60-Day Tightrope

For the estimated 600,000 Indian nationals currently working on H-1B visas in the United States, these layoffs are not merely career setbacks. They are existential crises. A laid-off H-1B holder has exactly 60 days to find a new sponsoring employer or leave the country. In a contracting market, that deadline is brutal. Surveys suggest nearly 45 per cent of Indian H-1B holders say they would return to India if laid off, citing visa instability as the primary reason.

The human cost is often invisible in the macro data. Dual-income couples where one spouse holds an H-1B and the other an H-4 dependent visa face simultaneous or back-to-back job losses. Families with children in American schools must weigh uprooting their lives against the ticking clock. Immigration lawyers report a measurable spike in stress-related consultations and emergency filings.

## A System Under Siege

The policy environment has only grown more hostile. The Trump administration's proposed 30 per cent wage increase for H-1B positions — open for public comment until 26 May — would raise salary floors significantly, making employers more selective and potentially pricing out junior roles that have historically served as entry points for Indian graduates. A new $100,000 application fee, imposed last September, has already dampened filing volumes.

Meanwhile, a raft of anti-H-1B legislation is moving through Congress. The "End H-1B Visa Abuse Act" and the "EXILE Act" propose freezing or severely curtailing the programme. Conservative commentators like Christopher Rufo have amplified the argument that H-1B visas depress domestic wages and enable outsourcing — a claim immigration advocates and most labour economists dispute.

## The Paradox That Won't Resolve

Amazon's situation encapsulates the paradox. The company is not, in any straightforward sense, "replacing" American workers with cheaper foreign ones. Its visa applications target specialised AI, cloud computing, and machine-learning roles — precisely the high-demand skills that its own efficiency drives are creating. The layoffs, meanwhile, have largely hit corporate operations, support, and legacy project teams.

But nuance does not travel well on social media. For millions of Americans watching tech jobs vanish while visa petitions pile up, the optics are damning. And for Indian workers — who account for roughly 70 per cent of all H-1B beneficiaries — the backlash feels deeply personal. They are caught between an industry that still needs their skills and a political climate that increasingly treats their presence as a grievance.

## Bengaluru as Plan B

The silver lining, if one can call it that, is that India's own technology ecosystem has matured enough to absorb returning talent. Global capability centres in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Pune are actively recruiting AI specialists at packages that, while lower in absolute terms, carry none of the visa anxiety. Several growth-stage Indian startups report that their best recent hires have been Silicon Valley returnees.

For the Indian diaspora in America, the message from 2026 is clear: the H-1B system, as currently constituted, offers neither the stability of permanent residency nor the flexibility of a genuinely portable career. Until Washington resolves that contradiction — or India's technology sector makes the question moot — hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals will continue living on a 60-day tightrope, one restructuring memo away from packing their bags.
